pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–6; Weather Forecasting & Safety (CONCEPTUAL, question-driven): ask questions to find out the PURPOSE of weather forecasting and how people prepare for and respond to severe weather.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation (Y1 'Seasonal changes') plus PSHE/keeping-safe; forecasting-as-preparation is cross-curricular at KS1. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS, ANCHOR): K-ESS3-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-2]' — the topic description mirrors this PE almost verbatim (NOT fetched this session → cited verified:false). DCI ESS3.B: [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-2] communities can prepare. The SEP is Asking Questions.
• Operational details — The payload is PURPOSE + PREPAREDNESS, not forecasting technique. Land two ideas: (1) a forecast tells us what the weather will PROBABLY do, so we can PLAN (take a coat, cancel the trip); (2) for severe weather (storm, flood, heat, blizzard) forecasts warn us so we can prepare and stay safe. Drive it through the child's own questions ('why do we watch the weather?', 'what do we do if a big storm is coming?'). Keep 'how forecasts are made' light (satellites/scientists watch the sky) — the mechanism is the 7-9 Weather Forecasting topic this feeds. Prerequisite: Seasonal changes. Evidence: forecasts help people plan/stay safe; describe preparing for ≥2 severe-weather types; ask relevant questions and find answers.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/observational): the child explains that a weather forecast helps people plan and stay safe, describes how people prepare for at least two kinds of severe weather, and asks relevant questions about weather and finds answers — focused on purpose and preparation, not on how forecasts are produced.
bestPractices: Centre the child's OWN questions (the PE's Asking-Questions practice): 'why do people check the weather?', 'what should we do if a storm is coming?' — then find answers together, modelling curiosity as the skill.
Make the forecast→decision link concrete: today's forecast shows rain → take a coat; a heatwave → hat, water, shade; a storm → stay indoors — purpose is seen in the action it prompts.
Cover at least two severe-weather types (per the evidence target) with simple, calm preparation steps, keeping the tone reassuring not frightening.
Frame a forecast as a PREDICTION ('probably', 'likely'), gently seeding that it isn't a guarantee — without over-explaining uncertainty at 5-6.
Connect to real routines children know (school closures for snow, a wet-play day, sun-cream days) so purpose is lived, not abstract.
Keep forecasting technique minimal here (weather scientists watch and measure the sky) and defer satellites/radar/models to the 7-9 topic.
keyRepresentations: A simple forecast card (today/tomorrow icons) paired with the action it prompts (coat, hat, stay-in).
A 'get ready' matching board: severe-weather warning → sensible preparation.
A question board where the child's own weather questions are posted and answered.
Calm before/after 'we were ready' scenes (prepared vs unprepared for the same forecast).
commonMisconceptions: 'The forecast/weather person MAKES the weather happen' — they predict and report it, they don't control it.
'A forecast is always exactly right' — it's a good prediction, not a guarantee; sometimes it changes.
'Severe weather is nothing to prepare for / always a disaster' — balance: storms can be serious, but preparing keeps us safe (reassurance).
'Checking the weather is just for fun' — its purpose is planning and safety.
'Weather and climate/season are the same' — a forecast is about the next day or two, not the whole season.

learn.summary: For ages 5–6, teach the PURPOSE of weather forecasting and severe-weather preparedness (not forecasting technique). Land two ideas: (1) a forecast tells us what the weather will PROBABLY do so we can PLAN (grab a coat, cancel a trip); (2) for severe weather (storm, flood, heat, blizzard) forecasts warn us so we can prepare and stay safe. Drive learning through the child's OWN questions ('why do we watch the weather?', 'what do we do if a big storm is coming?'), the Asking-Questions practice at the heart of this topic. The strongest route at this age enacts the forecast→decision→consequence loop so purpose is felt, not merely told; preparation matching and an in-role forecaster interview complement it; recognition checks verify the evidence targets. Keep 'how forecasts are made' light (scientists watch and measure the sky) and defer satellites/radar/models to a later 7–9 topic. Prerequisite: Seasonal changes.

activities.title: Plan the day from the forecast
feedback: When the right preparation is chosen: 'You checked the forecast and got ready — that's exactly why we look at the weather.'
When unprepared: 'The forecast said rain — without a coat the character got soaked. Next time, what could the forecast help you grab?' (reassuring, not frightening).
For the storm round: 'A storm warning means it's safest to stay indoors — being ready keeps us safe.'
activities.rationale: Using a forecast to make a decision and seeing the outcome makes 'why we forecast' concrete through consequence, which is well matched to a 5–6 year old's reliance on lived cause-and-effect over verbal explanation. An interactive decision surface (choose preparation, then watch the result) makes the purpose visible in a way a static description only tells about; this is offered as a strong fit, not a claim that a page cannot teach the idea. This method efficacy is a proposal, not validated.
learnerActions: Look at a simple forecast card (today/tomorrow with weather icons) that shows, e.g., heavy rain.
Decide what the character should grab or do before going out (just a t-shirt, or a coat and umbrella).
See the consequence play out: sent out coatless in the rain, the character comes back soaked and shivering; given a coat and umbrella, they stay dry and happy.
Repeat with a scorching-sun forecast (right call: sun hat, water, shade) and with a storm warning (safe call: stay indoors).
Each round, say in your own words WHY the forecast mattered — it let you get ready.
activities.intendedInsight: A forecast's purpose is seen in the action it prompts: knowing what the weather will probably do lets us prepare so the day goes well and we stay safe.

activities.title: Get-ready matching for severe weather
feedback: On a correct match: 'Yes — a heatwave warning means hat, water and shade. The forecast gave people time to get ready.'
On a mismatch: 'Let's think — in a flood, would staying low or moving to higher, dry ground be safer?' Keep the tone calm and reassuring.
Reinforce: 'Storms can be serious, but when we're prepared we can stay safe.'
activities.rationale: Covering at least two severe-weather types with calm preparation steps directly serves the evidence target while keeping the tone reassuring rather than alarming. Matching is a clean way to connect hazard to action; connecting to routines children already know makes the purpose lived rather than abstract. The effectiveness of this matching format is a proposal, not validated.
learnerActions: Match each severe-weather warning (storm, flood, heat wave, blizzard) to a sensible, calm preparation.
For at least two of these, say aloud one thing people do to stay safe and why.
Talk about a real routine you know that fits (a snow day closing school, a wet-play day, a sun-cream day).
activities.intendedInsight: Different severe weather calls for different, simple preparations; forecasts warn us ahead of time so communities can get ready and stay safe.

activities.title: Interview the weather presenter
feedback: Model curiosity: 'Great question! Let's find out together.'
Keep in-role answers short: 'I watch and measure the sky to work out what the weather will probably do, then tell you so you can get ready.'
If the child asks whether the presenter makes the weather: 'No — I only tell you what's likely. Saying it doesn't make it happen, like guessing a score before a game.'
activities.rationale: This topic explicitly centres the Asking-Questions practice; inviting and answering the child's own questions directly exercises it and serves the 'ask relevant questions and find answers' evidence target. A conversational in-role format lets purpose be stated and probed; it complements rather than replaces the consequence-based decision activity. The claim supports the Asking-Questions objective; the interaction's efficacy remains untested.
sourceClaims: K-ESS3-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-2].' DCI ESS3.B: [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-2]; scientists forecast severe weather so communities can prepare. (Topic description mirrors this PE.)
learnerActions: Post your own weather questions on a question board, e.g. 'why do people check the weather?', 'what should we do if a storm is coming?'
Ask a friendly weather-presenter character (a grown-up in role, or a classroom puppet/persona) your questions.
Listen to short, reassuring answers in role and ask a follow-up ('what if the forecast is wrong?').
Find and share one answer together from a sensible source.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientists forecast the weather so people can plan and stay safe; asking good questions and finding answers is how we learn about weather and hazards.

activities.title: Why do we check the forecast? (purpose check)
feedback: Addressing 'the forecaster makes it rain': 'The forecaster reads clues like the clouds and their measurements to guess what's coming — saying it doesn't make it happen.'
Addressing 'a forecast is always right': 'Forecasts give the most likely weather — usually right, not always, which is why they say "probably."'
Addressing 'forecasts are useless guesses': 'Knowing rain is likely still helps you pack a coat — being prepared beats being caught out.'
activities.rationale: Recognition items and a short discussion question check the evidence targets and surface the documented young misconception that a forecaster causes the weather. Recognition alone verifies understanding but does not elicit the child's own decision-making, so it is paired with the enactment and interview activities. This checking approach is a proposal, not validated.
learnerActions: Answer 'why do we check the weather forecast?' choosing from options (e.g. to plan and stay safe; just for fun; to make the weather happen).
Match a forecast to the preparation it should prompt.
Talk about this: 'The TV forecast said it will probably rain tomorrow. A child says the forecaster is making it rain. Is that right? What does a forecast actually do, and why is it useful?'
Say what you would do if the forecast said sun but it rained.
activities.intendedInsight: A forecaster predicts (not controls) the likely weather from clues; a forecast is a good prediction, not a guarantee, and its purpose is to help people plan and stay safe.

constraints: Payload is PURPOSE + PREPAREDNESS, not forecasting technique. Keep 'how forecasts are made' minimal (scientists watch and measure the sky); defer satellites, radar and models to a later 7–9 forecasting topic.
Cover at least two severe-weather types (storm, flood, heat wave, blizzard) with simple, calm preparation steps; keep the tone reassuring, never frightening.
Frame a forecast as a PREDICTION ('probably', 'likely'), gently seeding that it isn't a guarantee — without over-explaining uncertainty at 5–6.
Prerequisite: Seasonal changes. Distinguish a forecast (the weather for the next few days) from a whole season or climate.
Recognition/matching items verify the evidence targets but do not elicit the child's own decision-making or question-asking; pair them with the enactment and interview activities.

A static reveal scene of people preparing can serve as a useful reference, but it describes rather than lets the child decide and see the consequence; use it as a supporting reference, not the main vehicle for purpose.

Address common misconceptions directly: forecasters predict rather than control the weather; forecasts are likely not certain; severe weather is serious but preparation helps keep us safe; checking weather is for planning/safety, not just fun.

For any heat/sun preparation, observe safely: never ask a child to look at the sun or hold material toward the sun to check it; inspect the cast shadow or shaded ground instead. Keep heat prep to hat, water and shade.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched this session and remain unverified (verified:false in the source). Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both cited standards are marked verified:false in the source (NGSS K-ESS3-2 not fetched this session; DfE KS1/PSHE mapping from prior-session knowledge). The topic description reportedly mirrors the NGSS performance expectation almost verbatim; treat the exact wording as unconfirmed pending re-verification.

The UK state-tier standard mapping was marked DEFERRED in the source; UK home for 'forecasting-as-preparation' at KS1 is described as cross-curricular (weather observation + PSHE keeping-safe) rather than a single explicit standard.
Source confidence was logged as 'high' despite unverified sources; this rewrite does not upgrade or endorse that confidence.

The source rated a 3D format 'poor' as adding no spatial dimension; this has been treated as a format-selection note for this decision-based topic, not a universal claim that 3D cannot teach it, and is therefore not carried as a pedagogical law.

Minor conservative edit: the original storm advice 'stay indoors' is retained; for flood specifically the feedback nudges toward higher dry ground, since 'stay indoors' is not always correct for floods — kept simple and reassuring for age 5–6.

sourceClaims were set to [] for activities 1, 2 and 4 because their rationales are about the efficacy of specific interactions (consequence loop, matching, recognition check), which the standard claim does not support; only activity 3 retains the claim, where the Asking-Questions SEP it names directly supports the rationale. Efficacy of all proposed interactions remains untested.

probeDeeper: How do you think a forecaster works out what tomorrow's weather will be?
The forecast says a big storm is coming — name two things people could do to stay safe.
The forecast said sun but it rained — does that mean forecasts are useless? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the forecaster doesn't make the weather. They study clues, like the clouds and their measurements, to work out what the weather will PROBABLY do, and tell us ahead of time. It's useful because we can plan and stay safe — take a coat, or stay indoors in a storm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forecaster causes the weather — 'saying it will rain makes it rain'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate telling from causing: the forecaster reads clues to guess what's coming, like guessing the score before a game — saying it doesn't make it happen.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the forecaster makes it rain by saying it on TV.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the forecast brings the weather about rather than predicting it

errorPatterns.pattern: Forecasts are certain — 'if they said rain, it MUST rain'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce 'probably': forecasts give the most likely weather and are usually but not always right, which is why they say 'probably'.
errorPatterns.distractor: A forecast is always right — if they say rain, it will definitely rain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the forecast as a guarantee rather than a likelihood

errorPatterns.pattern: Forecasts are pointless guesses — 'you can't know the future so they don't help'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the value of likely-but-not-certain: knowing rain is likely still helps you pack a coat; being prepared beats being caught out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses forecasts as useless because they aren't certain

responseLevels.gap: Says the forecaster makes or controls the weather, or that forecasts are useless guesses.
responseLevels.full: Says forecasters predict (not cause) the likely weather from clues, that it's usually but not always right, and names ways it helps people plan and stay safe, handling a wrong-forecast case.
responseLevels.partial: Says a forecast tells us the weather ahead and helps us plan, but treats it as always correct or can't say how forecasters know.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The weather forecast on TV said it will probably rain tomorrow. A child says, 'So the weather forecaster is making it rain tomorrow.' Is that right? What does a weather forecast actually do, and why is it useful?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands forecasting says the forecaster predicts, not controls, the weather. A child with the causal confusion says the forecaster makes it rain — a documented young idea — and the follow-up shows whether they grasp the planning/safety purpose.
